1.pericope_label: King Arad attacks Israel, and the vow that gave Hormah its name

schools.summary: Gill collects the rival identifications of Arad from Jerome, Aben Ezra and Jarchi; Calvin argues at length against the Amalekite reading in favour of the Amorites, sees providence in Israel being tried by one nation rather than many, and defends the apparent cruelty of the vow by grounding it in a destruction God had already decreed.

Henry reads Arad's attack as a miscalculation that made his people the first of the Canaanites to fall rather than the last, makes the vow a pattern for asking mercy by binding ourselves to honour God with what we seek, and hears the name Hormah echoed in the Armageddon of the Revelation.

Clarke follows Kennicott in denying that the way of the spies can mean the route of the earlier spies and suspects the third verse was added after Joshua's day; Wesley takes the spies for scouts Israel sent to watch its own march and reads the initial defeat as humiliation meant to stop them trusting their own valour.

Keil and Delitzsch explain why Israel could defer the vow's execution, since Moses never intended to enter Canaan from the south; Ellicott re-renders the opening verse, leaves the date of the attack open, prefers to take Atharim as an otherwise unknown place, and notes that Hormah is used by anticipation earlier and probably renamed later.

debates: Whether Arad's people were Amalekites or Amorites, and whether their cities were destroyed then or long afterwards
outliers: Clarke suspects the third verse is a later addition by Joshua or Ezra, where the other sources read it as written

4.pericope_label: The fiery serpents and the serpent of brass

schools.summary: Calvin reads the loathing of manna as contempt for what is vile in their eyes, thinks the serpents were created for the occasion, makes the strangeness of the cure its whole point since faith must be willing to be foolish, and dissents from the common reading of the lifting up, referring it to the preaching of the gospel rather than the crucifixion; Gill hears a speaking against Christ in the murmuring and places the brass at the mines of Punon.

Henry asks what will please those whom manna will not please, finds justice in a thirst no water could quench, holds that God gives effectual relief in the best way though not in our way, and runs the typology through disease, remedy and application to the promise that a weak and weeping eye was healed as surely as any.

Clarke renders the scorned manna as cheat-stomach stuff, argues from Lucan for the prester or dipsas against Bochart's water-snake, and denies flatly that the brazen serpent was a type of Christ while granting five parallels from our Lord's words; Wesley sets out the correspondence of shape, pole and looking, and explains the delay as answering an incomplete humbling.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the Arabah as a desert that would furnish little but manna and make the cure depend on faith in the promise; Ellicott glosses the seraphim and their name, notes that venomous snakes still abound there, applies the contempt for manna to the modern church, and traces the serpent's preservation down to Hezekiah.

debates: Whether the brazen serpent was a type of Christ, and whether its lifting up figures the crucifixion or the preaching of the gospel
outliers: Clarke denies outright that the serpent was a type of Christ, against Henry, Wesley, Ellicott and Calvin, who all read it so

10.pericope_label: The stages to the plains of Moab, the book of the wars, and the well at Beer

schools.summary: Calvin denies that the phrase points to any book at all, reading it as saying the place would be celebrated whenever God's wars were recounted, takes Vaheb for a verb rather than a town so that Arnon answers the Red Sea, doubts the well is the old rock and explains Paul's following Rock as water drawn along after them, and contrasts princes digging by a touch of the staff with armies digging by labour; Gill reports Aben Ezra on the book and follows the Targums in reading the last verses of the well's own progress.

Henry reads the stages as a quickening near the journey's end, praises the scruple that spared Moab as Lot's posterity, makes much of a thirst borne without murmuring so that God gave before they asked, sets Oboth's scanty vessels against the well of heaven, and holds that the water was promised but the ground had still to be opened.

Clarke calls the Vaheb clause impenetrably obscure, reports Calmet's emendation of Zared for Vaheb and offers his own reading of it as a proverb of distance, prefers Lightfoot's account of the book as Moses' private directions for Joshua, and refuses the picture of princes digging with walking-sticks by re-translating the song; Wesley reconciles the commands about Moab and defends the quotation of an uncanonical book.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the ravine of the Arnon, dismiss two modern theories of the book in favour of odes from Moses' own time, and mark that Beer's water came by digging rather than by striking a rock; Ellicott notes the Hebrew leaves the bank of the encampment open, renders the lawgiver's direction as the ruler's staff, and reports the Targumic reading of the well's travels.

debates: What the book of the wars of the LORD was, and what 'Vaheb in Suphah' means
outliers: Clarke rejects the plain sense of the princes digging with their staves and re-translates the song accordingly; Calvin rejects the rendering 'book' that almost all translators give

21.pericope_label: Sihon refuses passage, and Israel takes the land of the Amorites

schools.summary: Calvin holds that God had not yet declared Israel masters east of Jordan and explains the destruction of the Amorite cities as policy rather than cruelty, denying a slothful people any comfortable resting-place short of Canaan; Gill traces Sihon's refusal past distrust to the hardening of his heart.

Henry contrasts Sihon's unprovoked sortie with Edom's mere refusal of passage, sees the enemies of the church infatuated in their own best counsels, and works out Israel's title twice over, against the Amorites by the grant made to Abraham and against Moab by the fact that the Amorites had taken the land first, drawing from it the wings that possessions make for themselves and a providence that lodged the country with trustees.
Wesley holds the offer of peace was meant in earnest, and reads the note about Ammon's border as explaining why Sihon could not push his conquests eastward rather than why Israel spared Ammon.

Keil and Delitzsch set the embassy beside the one to Edom, explain why war was commanded here and forbidden there, and fix the conquest between Arnon and the upper Jabbok; Ellicott makes the same point about Ammon's border and argues that dwelt should be sojourned, the permanent settlement east of Jordan coming only after Moses' death.

debates: Whether Israel settled the Amorite country at once or only encamped in it until after Moses' death

26.pericope_label: The proverb of Heshbon and the ballad of the Amorite conquest

schools.summary: Calvin argues Moses recorded Heshbon's earlier history to forestall the Ammonite claim Jephthah later answered, asks why Ammon rather than Moab pressed it and answers that plunderers glory in other men's rights, reads the ode as men summoning each other to Sihon's standard, and takes the lords of the high places for the idols themselves; Gill identifies the proverb-makers with Amorite poets who versified their wars as Homer did Troy.

Clarke derives the name of the proverb-makers from a root meaning to rule and ranks them with the poets of Greece and Rome, the Arab shaara and the Druid bards, dividing the ode into three parts printed from Kennicott; Wesley breaks with that division, holding the Amorite song ends before the woe on Moab and the rest is Israel's own comment, and closes on the shortness of the triumphing of the wicked.

Keil and Delitzsch count three strophes and identify Chemosh as the chief god of Moab and Ammon, which Jerome took for another name of Baal Peor; Ellicott holds again that the verb means sojourned rather than dwelt.

debates: Where the Amorite song ends and Israel's own comment on it begins
outliers: Wesley assigns the last two verses of the ode to the Israelites rather than to the Amorite poets, against Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch, who read them as strophes of the same song

32.pericope_label: Jaazer taken, and Og of Bashan destroyed at Edrei

schools.summary: Calvin reads the ease of the conquest as proof of favour, argues that Og would not have marched out unless he thought himself a match for Israel, and explains the destruction of so fertile a country as the only way of stopping a people who would otherwise have settled in it as in a delightful nest; Gill supplies Jerome's distances, Og's stature, and the sixty walled cities that fell to half Manasseh.

Wesley identifies Jaazer as another town Sihon had taken from Moab, suggests that Sihon and Og led two colonies out of Canaan, and describes Bashan's pastures and oaks; Clarke closes the chapter with Kennicott's long remarks, which take the way of the spies for a proper name, read Mattanah, Nahaliel and Bamoth as poetry rather than stations, and place Suph near the meeting of Arnon and Jordan.

Keil and Delitzsch observe that the starting point of the Bashan expedition is nowhere given because it did not matter to the writer's purpose, and treat the promise about Og as the counterpart of the promise about Sihon, with the ban executed alike on both.

debates: Whether Mattanah, Nahaliel and Bamoth are encampments or figures in a song
